intro: The second movement of the Second Symphony, “Resurrection”, follows the opening funeral march and is a dance for strings in A♭ major. At its first return the cellos add a new melody, and at the next the strings play the whole tune plucked.

B · Running triplets in the strings
sections.mNote: A horn introduces the minor-key episode.

sections.label: A′ · Dance theme with cello countermelody

cues.title: Ländler in A♭ major, strings
cues.text: The strings begin a Ländler, an Austrian country dance in three, in A♭ major after the first movement’s C minor. Mahler marks it Sehr gemächlich (very leisurely) and adds Nie eilen, never hurry.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, Hofmeister full score (1897), movement II, p. 57: A♭ major, 3/8, opening string parts and tempo directions.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Triplets in the strings, rehearsal 3
cues.text: A horn figure introduces running triplets. Only a few string desks play them at first, and more desks join as the figures continue. The tune has moved to the minor, but Mahler marks the passage “Nicht eilen. Sehr gemächlich.”
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, p. 58, rehearsal 3: horn figure, reduced string desks, triplets and Nicht eilen. Sehr gemächlich. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP415748-PMLP49406-GMahler_Symphony_No.2_fe_UE_reprint_RSL1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Steinbach am Attersee, July 1893
cues.text: At Steinbach am Attersee in July 1893, Mahler worked on three movements: this dance, the fish-sermon scherzo and Urlicht. He dated the Andante’s orchestral draft 30 July, eleven days after the song.
cues.evidence: Manuscript dates for the scherzo, Urlicht and Andante: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: Return of the Ländler, cello counter-melody
cues.text: The Ländler returns in A♭ major. The violins play the dance tune while the cellos add a new legato melody below it, and the double basses play the beat pizzicato.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 61–62, rehearsal 5: return to Tempo I, added cello line and pizzicato double basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Publication by Hofmeister, Leipzig
cues.text: With the support of two wealthy Hamburg industrialists, Hofmeister of Leipzig published the symphony first in Hermann Behn’s two-piano arrangement in 1896, then as a full score in February 1897.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling, essay for the Universal Edition study score (December 2010); the February 1897 date: Mahler Foundation, https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/. https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

cues.title: Return of the minor-key episode
cues.text: The minor-key episode returns, and winds and brass join the strings. The triplets now drive a full orchestral passage.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, second contrasting episode, pp. 64–72. The movement’s alternating dance and triplet sections are described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler’s letter of 1896
cues.text: In a letter of 1896 Mahler called the Andante and the Scherzo “episodes from the life of the fallen hero”. In the same letter he described the first movement as the hero’s titanic struggle with life and fate, and his death.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s letter of 1896 on the symphony, quoted by the Mahler Foundation: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-manuscript/

cues.title: Partial première, Berlin, 1895
cues.text: On 4 March 1895 Mahler conducted the first three movements in Berlin. The Andante and scherzo followed the funeral march, and the concert stopped there. Urlicht and the choral finale were first heard in public on 13 December 1895.
cues.evidence: Partial première on 4 March and complete première on 13 December 1895: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: Return of the Ländler, pizzicato
cues.text: The Ländler returns in A♭ major, played pizzicato by the strings. Flute, piccolo and harp add short notes above.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 73–74, rehearsal 12: Tempo I, pizzicato strings, piccolo, flute and harp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Steinbach am Attersee, June 1893
cues.text: By about 20 June 1893 Mahler and his household, Natalie Bauer-Lechner among them, had moved to Steinbach am Attersee. He worked first on this Andante and finished its sketch in about seven days. He had not yet orchestrated it.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling, essay for the Universal Edition study score of Symphony No. 2 (December 2010). https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Symphony-No.-2/P0049337

transitions.title: A horn starts the triplets
transitions.from: A · Ländler theme in A♭ major, strings
transitions.to: B · Running triplets in the strings
transitions.how: At rehearsal 3 the A♭-major dance moves to the minor. A soft horn figure starts the triplets, and at first only a few string desks join it. Flute, clarinet and harp enter later in the passage. The marking Nicht eilen is repeated in the score, and the beat stays at the opening tempo while the note values get shorter.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister full score (1897), movement II, p. 58, rehearsal 3; reduced string desks and Nicht eilen. Sehr gemächlich.

transitions.title: Cello countermelody under the returning Ländler
transitions.from: B · Running triplets in the strings
transitions.to: A′ · Dance theme with cello countermelody
transitions.how: The triplets slow and grow softer. At rehearsal 5, marked In Tempo I zurückkehren, the opening tempo returns with the A♭-major Ländler. The violins play the dance melody, the cellos play a sustained countermelody below it and the double basses continue pizzicato.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 61–62: rehearsal 5, In Tempo I zurückkehren, cello countermelody and pizzicato basses.

transitions.title: Winds and brass take up the triplets
transitions.from: A′ · Dance theme with cello countermelody
transitions.how: The second triplet episode brings winds and brass into the running string figures. The short notes, first played by a few players, now pass through the whole orchestra, and longer wind phrases are held above them.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 64–72, the expanded second triplet episode.

transitions.title: Return of the opening tempo, pizzicato
transitions.how: The running figures break into short fragments. At rehearsal 12 Mahler restores the opening tempo and A♭ major and marks the strings pizzicato. Flute, piccolo and harp decorate the plucked melody as it passes through the string sections.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement II, pp. 73–74, rehearsal 12 and the following Tempo I.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, full score (Hofmeister 1897; Weinberger/Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: Second movement, pp. 57–79: string Ländler, triplet episodes, added cello melody and the plucked return at rehearsal 12.

timeline.note: The strings begin the Ländler, with divided inner parts and a measured bass.
A horn starts the triplets with a few string desks; flute, clarinet and harp join them.
The dance returns with an expressive cello countermelody below the upper strings.
Winds and brass join the strings in the second triplet episode.
Flutes and violins play long phrases above divided strings playing triplets.
The strings pluck the returning dance; piccolo, flute and harp add short decorations.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
